blocks.text: The lawsuit filed in San Jose, Calif., on Monday accuses the CEO and his company of misleading shareholders by concealing the relationship with a woman accused of feeding information to Bejing, and not disclosing that the matter raised national security concerns ‌that threatened Nvidia's reputation and business prospects.
Lawsuit launched by an individual Nvidia shareholder on behalf of others who also own shares in the company
Nvidia and chief executive Jensen Huang were sued on Monday in a proposed class ‌action accusing them of defrauding shareholders by concealing Huang's ties with a suspected Chinese spy.

According to a complaint filed in federal court in San Jose, Calif., the defendants misled shareholders about Huang's alleged affair with Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based Megaspeed who is not related to him, and did not disclose that ⁠the matter raised ⁠national security concerns ‌that threatened Nvidia's reputation and business prospects.
The New York Times reported last month about the alleged relationship and that U.S. authorities had concluded Alice Huang was ⁠a Chinese intelligence asset.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Jensen Huang told Nvidia's employees he ‌had been unfaithful to his wife, without disclosing details of the alleged relationship.
The falling star of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang | About That

He co-founded Nvidia, and has led the Santa Clara, Calif.-based company as it became the world's most valuable chipmaker and made him one of the world's ⁠most prominent symbols of the artificial intelligence boom.

Nvidia announced ⁠a probe into the matter on Sunday. Its shares closed ⁠down ⁠4.3 per cent on Monday, reducing Nvidia's market capitalization by approximately $190 billion US. The lawsuit was filed five minutes after ⁠the U.S. stock market closed.

items: Could Nvidia survive without its ultra-powerful CEO, Jensen Huang?

blocks.text: It is common for shareholders to sue companies after unexpected share price declines. Nvidia shareholders led by Mark Kistenmacher are seeking unspecified damages from the defendants.

Kistenmacher seeks to represent anyone who bought shares of Nvidia between Oct. 9, 2025, and Nov. 8, 2026 — when the New York Times first reported about Huang's meeting with the supposed spy, and when Nvidia said it was launching an investigation regarding its CEO being the target of a foreign intelligence effort.
